counties.name: Denton
counties.blurb: Lake towns, horse ranches, and the fast-growing 35W corridor.

counties.name: Tarrant
counties.blurb: Cowtown grit, walkable mid-cities, and big-value neighborhoods.

counties.name: Wise
counties.blurb: Lakes, ranchland, and the pink courthouse — the metroplex’s western frontier.

counties.name: Collin
counties.blurb: Boomtown corridor — corporate HQs, top-rated schools, master plans.

counties.name: Dallas
counties.blurb: The urban core — skyline high-rises to first-ring family streets.

counties.name: Rockwall
counties.blurb: Lakeside living on Ray Hubbard’s east shore.

counties.name: Kaufman
counties.blurb: Room to grow east of the loop — new roofs, small-town squares.

counties.name: Ellis
counties.blurb: Rolling blackland prairie and courthouse-square towns.

cities.name: Sanger
cities.vibe: Sanger is the last small town before Lake Ray Roberts — a feed-store downtown, FFA barns, and I-35 running you into Denton in fifteen minutes. Lake weekends are the local currency.
hoods: The original grid off Bolivar Street

cities.name: Denton
cities.vibe: Denton runs on two universities, a legendary little music scene, and a courthouse square that stays busy after dark. Buyers get historic bungalows, duplex income plays, and new north-side master plans in a single market.
hoods: Historic bungalows walkable to the square

cities.name: Aubrey
cities.vibe: Aubrey is where the blackland prairie still shows — horse fences and feed stores beside brand-new master plans. You get small-town Friday nights with the Dallas North Tollway extension pulling the metroplex closer every year.
hoods: Resort-style master plan on the west side
Value-minded new builds off the DNT extension
Original grid, big trees, small-town bones

cities.name: Little Elm
cities.vibe: Little Elm wraps around Lewisville Lake with an actual beach, a boardwalk, and lakefront patios — rare things in North Texas. Prices run a meaningful step below Frisco next door, which keeps the growth coming.
hoods: Established value play east of the lake
Mature streets close to the shoreline

cities.name: The Colony
cities.vibe: The Colony pairs older, affordable lake-adjacent streets with Grandscape — one of the biggest retail-entertainment districts in the country. It’s the rare inner suburb where you can still find a deal walkable to something.

cities.name: Argyle
cities.vibe: Argyle is horse-property Texas with one of the state’s most sought-after small school districts. Custom homes on an acre or more, FFA trailers in the school lot, and Fort Worth or Denton twenty-odd minutes away.
hoods: Farm-themed master plan with community garden
Estate lots on the east side

cities.name: Northlake
cities.vibe: Northlake barely existed a decade ago; now Pecan Square and its neighbors are filling the 35W corridor with front-porch neighborhoods and event lawns. It’s new-build country with Fort Worth commutes.
hoods: Front-porch master plan, packed events calendar
Shared with Argyle — farmstand and all

cities.name: Lantana
cities.tagline: A golf-course village under the oaks
cities.vibe: Lantana is a single master-planned community that functions like its own town — golf course down the middle, pools and gyms in every village, and a fiercely loyal resident base. HOA-run and proud of it.
hoods: Family core near the amenity centers
Larger lots on the south side

cities.name: Highland Village
cities.vibe: Highland Village is a quiet, nearly built-out town on Lewisville Lake’s south shore — mature trees, top Lewisville ISD campuses, and The Shops giving it a retail heart. Inventory is scarce, and the neighbors prefer it that way.

cities.name: Trophy Club
cities.vibe: Built around the only golf course Byron Nelson ever designed, Trophy Club is mature trees, wide cul-de-sacs, and one of the metro’s best-regarded high schools. Fifteen minutes to DFW Airport without the flight path.

cities.name: Roanoke
cities.tagline: The Unique Dining Capital of Texas
cities.vibe: Roanoke turned its brick Oak Street into a destination restaurant row — the state made the “Unique Dining Capital” title official. Behind the patios: new family streets, Byron Nelson schools, and the 114 corridor’s job engine.
hoods: Amenity pocket near Byron Nelson High

cities.name: Flower Mound
cities.vibe: Flower Mound is the polished suburban benchmark of Denton County — 60+ miles of trails, strict development standards, and schools that anchor resale values. The River Walk district added patios and canals to the formula.
hoods: Newer trail community to the west
Family staple with pools and ponds

cities.name: Lewisville
cities.tagline: Old Town on the lake’s doorstep
cities.vibe: Lewisville put a stage, breweries, and a rail stop in Old Town and let the lake do the rest. It’s the affordable heart of the Denton County boom — twenty minutes to DFW Airport without touching a tollbooth.
hoods: Golf master plan with its own gravity

cities.name: Decatur
cities.vibe: Decatur is Wise County’s heart — a working courthouse square in pink granite, with coffee, boots, and biscuits where US-287 crosses 380. Acreage buyers get real country with Fort Worth forty minutes down the road.
hoods: Victorian blocks around the pink courthouse
Newer builds on the west side

cities.name: Bridgeport
cities.vibe: Bridgeport is the west-side lake town — weekend cabins turned year-round customs on Lake Bridgeport, and a revived brick strip along Halsell Street. Prices here are the county’s most approachable.

cities.name: Rhome
cities.vibe: Rhome sits where 287 meets 114, which makes it Wise County’s fastest on-ramp to the metroplex. Northwest ISD zoning and new-build subdivisions are pulling first-time buyers across the Tarrant line.

cities.name: Boyd
cities.vibe: Boyd is a one-stoplight town on the Trinity’s west fork where FFA still outranks HOA. Buyers come for the acreage, stay for the quiet, and commute down 114.

cities.name: Aurora
cities.vibe: Aurora is the hamlet with the 1897 UFO legend and some of the county’s prettiest rolling acreage. No subdivisions to speak of — just long driveways and wide skies, fifteen minutes from Texas Motor Speedway.

cities.name: Celina
cities.vibe: Celina has been America’s fastest-growing city more than once, and the square still does Friday-night markets like the boom never happened. Buy here for the trajectory: the DNT is arriving, and so is everyone else.
hoods: Resort amenities on the east side
The square — markets and main-street brick

cities.name: Anna
cities.vibe: Anna is where Collin County still starts under $400K. US-75 runs straight to it, the new-build inventory is deep, and the city is racing to add the retail and parks its rooftops demand.

cities.name: Melissa
cities.vibe: Melissa keeps a one-district, one-town identity while doubling in size — the cardinal-red water tower says as much. It’s the tidy middle option between McKinney prices and Anna distances.

cities.name: Prosper
cities.vibe: Prosper made its name on quarter-acre-plus lots and a school district families chase across state lines. Windsong Ranch’s crystal lagoon set the amenity arms race; the town still insists on its small-town seal.
hoods: Newer luxury phases off the DNT

cities.name: McKinney
cities.vibe: McKinney’s historic square is the best downtown in the northern suburbs — working courthouse, wine bars, and a farmers market with a line. Around it: everything from 1900s bungalows to golf-course master plans.
hoods: TPC golf and the corporate corridor

cities.name: Frisco
cities.vibe: Frisco built the playbook every suburb now copies: pro sports as city planning. The Star, PGA headquarters, and a school district that opens a new campus most years. Master-planned to the last median — and it works.
hoods: The new north side, wrapped around PGA HQ

cities.name: Fairview
cities.vibe: Fairview holds the line at half-acre lots and dark-sky ordinances while Allen and McKinney boom on either side. The Lovejoy ISD half of town is one of the metro’s quietest luxury markets.

cities.name: Allen
cities.vibe: Allen runs one giant high school on purpose — the $60M stadium tells you how that’s going. Underneath the football is a genuinely complete suburb: watters Creek shopping, mature neighborhoods, easy 75 access.

cities.name: Lucas
cities.vibe: Lucas is one-acre-minimum country inside the Collin County boom — barns, pools, and long driveways, fifteen minutes from Allen’s big-box everything. Lovejoy ISD keeps demand permanently ahead of supply.

cities.name: Parker
cities.vibe: Parker is the town where Southfork Ranch sits — which tells you the look: white fences, long horizons, million-dollar ranchettes minutes from Plano. No commercial strip, and residents like it that way.

cities.name: St. Paul
cities.vibe: St. Paul is barely a square mile of quiet streets tucked between Wylie and Lucas — one of Collin County’s smallest towns and determined to stay that way. Large lots, low turnover, zero retail.

cities.name: Plano
cities.vibe: Plano is the suburb that already made it: Fortune 500 headquarters, the Legacy West district, and forty years of neighborhoods that hold value like index funds. Mature trees, remodeled ranches, and everything within 15 minutes.
hoods: High-rise living over shops and HQs
Estate blocks near the mall’s rebirth

cities.name: Murphy
cities.vibe: Murphy is a bedroom community in the truest sense — big brick homes on 8,000-plus-foot lots, Plano ISD zoning on the west side, and almost nothing to do after 9pm. That’s the pitch, and it lands.
hoods: Trail-laced with a big amenity center

cities.name: Wylie
cities.vibe: “Wide Awake Wylie” kept its brick downtown on Ballard Avenue and grew a real city around it. Two lakes on either side, a hometown school district, and prices that undercut the DNT corridor by $150K.

cities.name: Princeton
cities.vibe: Princeton has doubled in a decade as US-380 turned into a rooftop conveyor belt. Lakes on both sides and Collin County addresses keep the pipeline full.

cities.name: Farmersville
cities.vibe: Farmersville’s Onion Shed market square and Audie Murphy heritage anchor the county’s eastern holdout. Acreage buyers, this is the corner — the Chaparral rail-trail runs right through it.
hoods: Onion Shed square and brick storefronts

cities.name: Lavon
cities.vibe: Lavon sits at the foot of its namesake lake where Collin County still sells starter square footage. Grand Heritage’s flags mark the metro’s northeast growth edge.

cities.name: Nevada
cities.vibe: Nevada — locals say nev-AY-duh — is blackland-prairie quiet a mile from the growth front. Acre lots and metal-roof customs while the getting’s good.

cities.name: Fort Worth
cities.vibe: Fort Worth is the last big American city that still feels like itself — stockyards and honky-tonks, a world-class museum district, and neighborhoods from craftsman Fairmount to ranch-house Tanglewood at half of Dallas prices.

cities.name: Arlington
cities.vibe: Arlington stacks AT&T Stadium, Globe Life Field, and Six Flags into one entertainment district, with a huge spread of honestly-priced neighborhoods around it. UTA keeps the middle of the city young; Viridian is rewriting the north side.
hoods: Lakes, a sailing center, master-plan north

cities.name: North Richland Hills
cities.vibe: North Richland Hills is the mid-cities workhorse — NRH2O summers, TEXRail straight into DFW Airport, and block after block of solid brick inventory. Hometown’s canal-side cottages give it a new-urbanist heart.
hoods: Old-town grid at the TEXRail stop

cities.name: Lake Worth
cities.vibe: Lake Worth is a pocket-sized city on its namesake lake, minutes from the Naval Air Station and downtown Fort Worth. Modest ranch homes, boat slips, and some of Tarrant County’s most approachable prices.

cities.name: Azle
cities.vibe: Azle is the little lake city on Eagle Mountain’s west shore — boat dealers on Main Street, Cross Timbers acreage out the back door, and downtown Fort Worth twenty-odd minutes down 199.
hoods: Boat docks off Boat Club Road

cities.name: Keller
cities.vibe: Keller balances a walkable Old Town strip with half-acre neighborhoods that still feel semi-rural. Keller ISD’s reputation and quick 114 access to the airport keep it on nearly every northeast-Tarrant shortlist.
hoods: Walk to the town center strip

cities.name: Southlake
cities.vibe: Southlake is the metroplex’s benchmark luxury suburb: Carroll ISD’s Dragons, Town Square’s open-air brick blocks, and estate neighborhoods where teardowns start at seven figures. Five minutes to DFW’s north entrance.
hoods: Golf and pools, walkable to schools

cities.name: Grapevine
cities.vibe: Grapevine’s historic Main Street — wine rooms, the vintage railroad, a real ice cream parlor — sits ten minutes from every gate at DFW. Lakefront trails on one side, Christmas-capital energy all December.
hoods: Main Street porches and tasting rooms
Near the lake and the resorts

cities.name: Colleyville
cities.vibe: Colleyville is what quiet money buys in northeast Tarrant: gated courts, acre lots under mature oaks, and no through-traffic to speak of. The restaurant row along Colleyville Boulevard keeps it from being sleepy.

cities.name: Bedford
cities.vibe: Bedford is the mid-cities value thesis: 1980s brick homes with real trees, equidistant to both downtowns, and a 10-minute run to DFW Airport. Remodel inventory does brisk business here.

cities.name: Euless
cities.vibe: Euless sits at the geographic center of the metroplex, and the market knows it — starter homes and townhomes move in under a month. Trinity High’s legendary Polynesian football pipeline is a genuine point of pride.

cities.name: Hurst
cities.vibe: Hurst is the oldest of the HEB trio and prices like it — solid mid-century ranches, mature pecans, and the NE Mall retail engine. A remodeler’s market fifteen minutes from either downtown’s paycheck.

cities.name: Westlake
cities.vibe: Westlake routinely posts the highest median home price in Texas — Vaquero’s guard-gated Fazio golf estates set the tone, and the town-run Westlake Academy is a free IB school with a waitlist to match.

cities.name: Mansfield
cities.vibe: Mansfield is the southeast Tarrant magnet: a historic Main Street getting new patios and a school district families cross the metro for. Master plans keep landing along the 287 corridor.

cities.name: Benbrook
cities.vibe: Benbrook tucks between its namesake lake and Fort Worth’s southwest hills — horse trails, ridge-line streets, and a fifteen-minute run downtown. The quiet-value corner of Tarrant County.

cities.name: Burleson
cities.vibe: Burleson runs Old Town storefronts against fast new master plans down 35W. It’s Fort Worth’s southern release valve — schools, chains, and starter square footage in every direction.

cities.name: Saginaw
cities.vibe: Saginaw grew from rail-and-grain town into a full family suburb without losing its blue-collar practicality. Quick 287 access and Eagle Mountain water weekends seal it.

cities.name: Crowley
cities.vibe: Crowley sits south of Fort Worth with rail-town bones and a fresh wave of family subdivisions. Chisholm Trail Parkway put it fifteen minutes from downtown, and everyone noticed.

cities.name: Watauga
cities.vibe: Watauga packs parks, a library everyone brags about, and tidy 80s brick into four flat square miles. The definition of unpretentious Mid-Cities value.

cities.name: Haltom City
cities.vibe: Haltom City is Fort Worth’s scrappy northeast neighbor — post-war bungalows, the metro’s best Vietnamese food row on Belknap, and prices the inner ring can’t beat.

cities.name: White Settlement
cities.vibe: White Settlement grew up alongside the bomber plant and still runs on Lockheed shift changes. Modest brick, mighty location: ten minutes to downtown Fort Worth.

cities.name: Coppell
cities.vibe: Coppell is a school-district town with a farmers-market heart, boxed in by the airport and three highways — which is exactly why inventory stays scarce. Old Town’s cottages and porches carry the brand.

cities.name: Irving
cities.vibe: Irving is two cities: Las Colinas’ canals, corporate towers, and the Toyota Music Factory on one side; original 1950s neighborhoods reinventing themselves on the other. Nowhere in DFW is better connected.

cities.name: Dallas
cities.vibe: Dallas contains fifty markets in one: Lakewood Tudors, Bishop Arts bungalows, Uptown high-rises, Preston Hollow estates. If you want walkability, architecture, or a skyline view, this is where the metroplex keeps it.

cities.name: Sachse
cities.vibe: Sachse straddles the Dallas–Collin county line and quietly delivers what its flashier neighbors charge more for: newer brick homes, the PGBT a minute away, and The Station district finally giving it a downtown.
hoods: Golf community spilling in from Wylie

cities.name: Rowlett
cities.vibe: Rowlett owns more Lake Ray Hubbard shoreline than anyone, and the Bayside peninsula is slowly becoming the waterfront district it was always supposed to be. DART rail downtown is the quiet superpower.

cities.name: Grand Prairie
cities.vibe: Grand Prairie stretches from Joe Pool Lake to the entertainment district it shares with Arlington, with master plans like Mira Lagos stacked in between. Twenty minutes from either downtown — that’s the whole pitch.
hoods: Lakeside master plan on Joe Pool

cities.name: Garland
cities.vibe: Garland is a quarter-million people of first-ring value — Firewheel’s golf-course streets, a downtown square with DART rail, and mile after mile of solid 80s brick still trading under the metro median.

cities.name: Richardson
cities.vibe: Richardson pairs UT Dallas and the Telecom Corridor with some of the metro’s best mid-century housing stock. Duck Creek greenbelts, four DART stations, and a Chinatown food scene that punches far above the city’s size.

cities.name: Carrollton
cities.vibe: Carrollton spreads across three counties with the green line anchoring a walkable old downtown square. The Korean food corridor on Old Denton is a metro-wide draw, and the housing runs 70s ranch to new-build townhome.

cities.name: Farmers Branch
cities.vibe: Farmers Branch spent a decade planting restaurants and rail stops in what was pure office park, and the old core has real momentum now. Mid-century ranches on big lots still price under the neighbors.

cities.name: Addison
cities.tagline: A restaurant row with a runway
cities.vibe: Addison packs an airport, a circle, and roughly 180 restaurants into four square miles. Townhomes and condos dominate — the metro’s easiest lock-and-leave with a tollway address.

cities.name: Mesquite
cities.vibe: Mesquite keeps the metro’s east side honest: a real rodeo, real neighborhoods, and some of the last sub-$300K brick this close to the core. The 635/80 interchange puts both downtowns within reach.

cities.name: Duncanville
cities.tagline: City of Champions, priced to win
cities.vibe: Duncanville’s basketball banners are real, and so is the value: solid 70s and 80s brick in the shadow of the Cedar Ridge escarpment, ten miles from downtown Dallas.

cities.name: DeSoto
cities.vibe: DeSoto rolls over actual hills in southern Dallas County, with estate pockets that surprise first-time visitors. It’s the anchor of the Best Southwest and prices like the metro’s last deal.

cities.name: Cedar Hill
cities.vibe: Cedar Hill owns the highest ground between the Red River and the Gulf, with a state park on Joe Pool Lake and switchback streets that don’t feel like Dallas at all.

cities.name: Lancaster
cities.vibe: Lancaster’s 1850s town square is the South Dallas County keeper, and the runway-adjacent logistics boom is bringing rooftops with it. Value hunters should look now.

cities.name: Balch Springs
cities.vibe: Balch Springs is one of the metro’s true entry points — post-war brick and newer infill where first-time buyers still pencil out, minutes from the 635/20 interchange.

cities.name: Sunnyvale
cities.vibe: Sunnyvale is Dallas County’s quiet exception: one-acre zoning, a top-rated small district, and pasture views fifteen minutes from downtown. Supply is thin and stays that way on purpose.

cities.name: Seagoville
cities.vibe: Seagoville keeps a farm-town gait inside Dallas County lines — big lots, big trucks, and Trinity bottomland to the south. New builds are finding it fast.

cities.name: Rockwall
cities.tagline: Harbor lights east of the lake
cities.vibe: Rockwall’s Harbor district — lighthouse, boardwalk, restaurants on the water — gives the east side of the lake a downtown to be proud of. Add a courthouse square and top-third schools, and it sells itself.

cities.name: Heath
cities.vibe: Heath is Rockwall County’s estate tier: golf-and-yacht-club living, acre lots rolling down to the water, and a strict no-hurry attitude toward development. The lagoon community brought the first real new-build wave.

cities.name: Fate
cities.vibe: Fate went from a blinking light to a boomtown on the strength of Woodcreek’s endless phases. Rockwall-adjacent value with I-30 access.

cities.name: Royse City
cities.vibe: Royse City kept its brick Main Street while the I-30 rooftops multiplied around it. The last stop before the metro hands off to the blackland — and prices show it.

cities.name: Forney
cities.vibe: Forney — the official Antique Capital of Texas — is now one of the metro’s fastest-growing value markets. Master plans line US-80, and buyers get 2,500 square feet for what a starter costs inside the loop.

cities.name: Terrell
cities.tagline: Rails, wings, and a real Main Street
cities.vibe: Terrell was a rail boomtown, trained British pilots in WWII, and kept the Main Street to prove it. The US-80 corridor is pulling the metro east to meet it.

cities.name: Kaufman
cities.vibe: Kaufman keeps a working courthouse square forty minutes from downtown Dallas. Land is the play here — the metro’s southeast growth arrow points straight at it.

cities.name: Crandall
cities.vibe: Crandall is where the US-175 growth wave lands next — master plans like Heartland brought thousands of rooftops, and the old four-corners town is figuring out its new size.

cities.name: Midlothian
cities.vibe: Midlothian built the concrete that built the metroplex; now it’s building neighborhoods — acre lots and new master plans on the rolling southwest edge, with both downtowns a straight 35-minute shot away.

cities.name: Waxahachie
cities.vibe: Waxahachie’s courthouse square and gingerbread Victorians make it the prettiest county seat in North Texas, and the I-35E growth wave has officially arrived. Old charm, new rooftops.

cities.name: Red Oak
cities.vibe: Red Oak is where the southern growth wave crosses the county line — new schools, new rooftops, and I-35E straight into downtown Dallas in under half an hour.

cities.name: Ovilla
cities.vibe: Ovilla is an old settlement of church steeples and acre-plus lots on the Ellis–Dallas line. Custom-home country that never got in a hurry.

cities.name: Glenn Heights
cities.vibe: Glenn Heights straddles the Dallas–Ellis line with some of the metro’s most attainable new construction. It’s growing fast and still feels like a small town on Sunday.

cities.name: Ennis
cities.vibe: Ennis throws the state’s official Bluebonnet Trails festival every April and drag-races all summer. A Czech-heritage downtown and true small-city prices anchor the metro’s southeast edge.

newBuilds.name: Pecan Square
newBuilds.note: Front-porch streets, a coworking barn, and a packed events lawn.

newBuilds.name: Sandbrock Ranch
newBuilds.note: Resort pool, fishing lakes, and an on-site elementary.

newBuilds.name: Union Park
newBuilds.note: Hilltop amenity village with a 35-acre central park off 380.

newBuilds.name: Harvest
newBuilds.note: The farm-themed plan — community garden, farmstand, and all.

newBuilds.name: Walsh
newBuilds.note: Fiber-first master plan on 7,200 west-side acres.

newBuilds.name: Viridian
newBuilds.note: Lakes, a sailing center, and River Legacy trail links.

newBuilds.name: Ventana
newBuilds.note: Rolling-hill value southwest of the 820 loop.

newBuilds.name: Shale Creek
newBuilds.note: Northwest ISD value at the 287/114 junction.

newBuilds.name: Sunset Ridge
newBuilds.note: New rooftops a mile from the pink courthouse.

newBuilds.name: Fields
newBuilds.note: Wrapped around the new PGA of America headquarters.

newBuilds.name: Light Farms
newBuilds.note: Trail-laced plan with its own on-site elementary.

newBuilds.name: Windsong Ranch
newBuilds.note: The crystal lagoon that started the amenity arms race.

newBuilds.name: Trinity Falls
newBuilds.note: Riverside trails and pocket parks up US-75.

newBuilds.name: Anacapri
newBuilds.note: Lagoon living at Collin County’s entry price.

newBuilds.name: Harmony Hill
newBuilds.note: New streets a minute off the PGBT.

newBuilds.name: The Station
newBuilds.note: Townhomes in the new town-center district.

newBuilds.name: Gateway Parks
newBuilds.note: Deep value and stacked amenities east on US-80.

newBuilds.name: Heath Golf & Yacht Club
newBuilds.note: Fairways and a lagoon above Ray Hubbard.
